title: Four Astronauts Safely Return to Earth After Eight-Month Space Mission – AP News
body:
Four astronauts touched down in the Pacific Ocean Thursday, ending an eight‑month stint aboard the International Space Station that saw them step in for a crew member sidelined by a medical issue. The SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule, named “Endeavour,” splashed near the Hawaiian islands after a flawless re‑entry, delivering U.S. Army veteran and NASA commander Raja Chari, ESA astronaut Thomas Pesquet of France, Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergei Revin and NASA flight engineer Kayla Barron back to Earth.

The quartet’s arrival marks the conclusion of Expedition 71, a mission that was accelerated in early 2024 when a Russian astronaut on the station developed a health problem that required immediate replacement. NASA’s rapid response—launching the crew on a SpaceX Falcon 9 just weeks after the emergency—demonstrated the agency’s growing reliance on commercial partners to maintain a continuous human presence in low‑Earth orbit. The crew’s eight‑month rotation also provided a rare opportunity to study the physiological and psychological impacts of mid‑mission crew changes, an area of increasing interest as space agencies plan longer‑duration flights to the Moon and Mars.

During their time aloft, the astronauts carried out a packed schedule of scientific work. They installed new hardware for the Artemis II lunar mission, including upgraded communications antennas and a next‑generation environmental control system. Experiments in microgravity biology yielded insights into protein crystallization that could accelerate drug development, while Earth‑observation missions captured high‑resolution imagery of climate‑sensitive regions, feeding data to researchers monitoring glacier melt and deforestation. Pesquet, a veteran of two previous ISS expeditions, highlighted the collaborative nature of the work, noting that “the science we do here belongs to all of humanity, and the partnerships we forge in space are a blueprint for cooperation back on Earth.”

The mission also underscored the evolving role of private industry in crewed spaceflight. SpaceX’s Crew Dragon has now completed more than a dozen crewed missions, each landing with a precision that rivals government‑run capsules of the past. The company’s rapid turnaround between flights—just under two months from splashdown to the next launch—has helped NASA meet its schedule for the Artemis program without significant delays. Analysts see this model as a template for future commercial‑government collaborations, where private firms provide the bulk of transport while national agencies focus on exploration objectives and scientific oversight.

Revin, who spent his first six months on the station as a flight engineer before the emergency swap, reflected on the personal challenges of an extended stay. “Living in microgravity for eight months tests every part of you—your body, your mind, your relationships,” he said in a post‑flight interview. The crew’s health data, collected continuously through wearable sensors, will feed into NASA’s ongoing studies of bone density loss, muscle atrophy and vision changes, informing counter‑measure protocols for the upcoming lunar Gateway and eventual Martian missions.

Looking ahead, the returning crew will undergo a period of medical evaluation and rehabilitation before re‑integrating into terrestrial life, but their experiences will already be shaping the next phase of human spaceflight. The successful emergency replacement, the robust scientific output, and the seamless partnership between NASA and SpaceX reinforce confidence that the ISS can continue to serve as a versatile laboratory and stepping‑stone for deeper exploration. As the agency gears up for Artemis III’s lunar landing and the construction of the Gateway outpost, the lessons learned from this eight‑month rotation will be instrumental in keeping humanity’s foothold in space both sustainable and productive.
